before: Case-level quality estimation without a new manual mask has been studied with reverse classification accuracy [3]. For promptable models, Kinalioglu combined mask changes under small prompt perturbations with model confidence for failure screening [4]. Loke et al. directly compared prompt-perturbation uncertainty with predicted IoU in SAM/MedSAM; most case-level differences remained unresolved after paired testing and multiplicity correction [5]. These studies motivate a separate operating question: a score can be evaluated by transferring a numerical cutoff or by allocating the same number of reviews. The former preserves a development operating rule; the latter compares rankings at a specified capacity. Their implications for detection and workload need to be distinguished when scores are transferred between datasets.
after: Reverse classification accuracy estimates case-level segmentation quality without a new manual mask [3]. Kinalioglu combined structural prompt responses with confidence and reported failure recovery among the highest-risk 10 % of masks [4]. Loke et al. compared prompt-perturbation uncertainty with predicted IoU, entropy and test-time augmentation across SAM/MedSAM using paired tests and multiplicity control [5]. Building on these scoring and ranking studies, we examine development-calibrated numerical cutoff transfer to internal and external breast ultrasound cohorts. Comparisons at the same actual review counts and joint reporting of detection, workload and misses distinguish cutoff transfer from capacity-constrained ranking.

before: We repeated detection analyses with reference Dice cutoffs of 0.50 and 0.80 while retaining both locked risk thresholds. We also ranked the external cases by each risk score and selected the top 50 per method, the count closest to a 20 % review fraction among 252 cases. Risk ties followed the unmodified archived patient-identifier strings in lexicographic order (for example, "1", "10", "100"), rather than numeric or zero-padded image-identifier order. This equal-review comparison used a common number of reviews in the observed external cohort; its paired interval is conditional on the observed rankings.

before: The following exploratory analyses were specified for this revision after the original study. They retain the original scores, low-quality definition and H1–H3. We examined development review targets of 5 %, 10 %, 15 %, 20 %, 25 %, 30 %, 40 % and 50 %, calibrating a separate threshold for each method with the same tied-group and nearest-target rules. Selection used development risks and counts, without quality labels. Each numerical threshold was transferred unchanged to both test cohorts. A separate equal-review policy selected the nearest integer to the target fraction of each test cohort, taking fewer cases at an exact half-integer tie.
after: After the original study, we conducted additional post hoc policy and diagnostic-accounting analyses. These retain the original scores, low-quality definition and H1–H3. We examined development review targets of 5 %, 10 %, 15 %, 20 %, 25 %, 30 %, 40 % and 50 %, calibrating a separate threshold for each method with the same tied-group and nearest-target rules. Selection used development risks and counts, without quality labels. Each numerical threshold was transferred unchanged to both test cohorts. A separate equal-review policy selected the nearest integer to the target fraction of each test cohort, taking fewer cases at an exact half-integer tie.

Post hoc descriptive readouts were taken at 33 and 35 reviews per method, the two external volumes produced by the transferred cutoffs; the 50-review readout repeated the original-protocol supplementary budget. All were extracted from the archived external ranking curves without new inference, calibration, intervals or hypothesis tests. The original contrasts and intervals remain unchanged.

At matched counts of either 33 or 35 reviews, A detected 10/16 low-quality masks and B detected 13/16, retaining the three-case difference observed at transferred cutoffs (Table S4 and Figure 4D). Increasing the common budget from 35 to 50 added four low-quality detections for A and none for B. The ordering therefore also varied with budget under the same ranking rule. These post hoc readouts describe this cohort without establishing population-level superiority.

before: A fixed numerical cutoff and a fixed review count make different commitments when a quality-control score is transferred. A cutoff can be applied case by case, leaving the resulting review fraction as an outcome. Ranking fixes the number selected within a defined cohort or batch. In the 20 %-target example, B detected 13/16 low-quality external masks at its transferred cutoff and A detected 10/16; at 50 reviews each, the counts were 13/16 and 14/16. The complete budget scan showed that this ordering depended on the target as well as the rule. Evaluating both policies therefore distinguishes the transfer of a development operating point from detection at a specified review capacity.
after: A numerical cutoff preserves a development decision threshold, whereas ranking at a fixed count allocates a specified number of reviews within a cohort or batch. In BrEaST, the transferred cutoffs selected 35 patients with A and 33 with B. At matched counts of either 33 or 35, B still detected 13/16 low-quality masks and A detected 10/16; the count difference at the cutoffs therefore was not explained solely by their unequal review volumes. At 50 reviews each, A detected 14/16 and B detected 13/16. The ordering also changed as the budget varied under the same equal-review ranking rule. Reporting the numerical cutoff, actual review count, detections and misses together makes both the operating rule and its budget explicit, without attributing the ordering change to policy alone.

before: Confidence and prompt disagreement capture different properties of the same initial prediction. A uses the model quality estimate, whereas B probes stability under four specified box translations. The replay contours make their shared blind spot visible: a consistently selected region can remain poorly aligned with the reference. Case175 is an inspectable example of this behavior, with a narrow upper-edge prediction and very low reference Dice. Prior work combined structural responses with confidence [4] and directly compared perturbation uncertainty with predicted IoU [5]. The present evaluation complements those approaches by jointly reporting detection, review volume and misses under explicit operating policies.
after: Confidence and prompt disagreement capture different properties of the same initial prediction. Budget-constrained failure screening is already established [4], as are cross-dataset and prompt-regime comparisons of uncertainty scores [5]. Here, the transferred cutoff leaves workload as an outcome, while equal-count ranking fixes the number selected. Our resampling routes separate calibration and test-sampling uncertainty. The matched-count readouts further identify budget-dependent ordering within this operating example.

before: Figure 4.  Risk-ranked review curves and external paired contrasts. Panels A and B show empirical step curves of the fraction of low-quality patients detected versus the actual number selected for simulated review, ranked by descending risk with official CaseID as the lexicographic tie-breaker. The cohorts contain 93/851 and 16/252 low-quality patients, respectively (Dice <0.70). Blue solid and orange dashed curves represent Methods A and B. Filled squares mark the development-locked cutoffs (internal A: 71/93 detected at 174 reviews; B: 68/93 at 150; external A: 10/16 at 35; B: 13/16 at 33). Open circles mark 50 external reviews per method (A: 14/16; B: 13/16). Panel C shows B minus A detection differences with the original paired nominal 95 % Newcombe method 10 intervals: +18.75 [−4.28, +40.04] percentage points at locked cutoffs and −6.25 [−31.61, +19.57] at top 50. The latter interval conditions on the observed ranking and does not account for re-ranking in another sample.
after: Figure 4.  Risk-ranked review curves, original paired contrasts and matched counts. A/B: internal (93 low-quality/851 patients) and external (16/252) curves, ranked by descending risk and lexicographic CaseID. Low quality is Dice <0.70. Blue solid/circle and orange dashed/triangle encodings identify A and B. Filled squares mark locked cutoffs: internal A, 71/93 at 174 reviews; B, 68/93 at 150; external A, 10/16 at 35; B, 13/16 at 33. Open circles mark 50 external reviews per method (A: 14/16; B: 13/16). C: B-minus-A detection differences with original paired nominal 95 % Newcombe method 10 intervals: +18.75 [−4.28, +40.04] percentage points at locked cutoffs and −6.25 [−31.61, +19.57] at top 50. The top-50 interval conditions on observed rankings. D: detection counts at the same external K (A/B: 10/13 at 33 and 35; 14/13 at 50), each among 16 low-quality patients. K33/35 are post hoc archived-curve readouts; K50 is the original-protocol supplementary budget. No new interval or test is assigned to D.

before: Table S4.  BrEaST performance at equal review volume
Each method selected 50 of the 252 scored cases in descending risk order. Ties followed lexicographic case identifier order. Low quality used reference Dice below 0.70.

Among the 16 low-quality cases, both methods flagged 12, only A flagged 2, only B flagged 1, and neither flagged 1. The paired B-minus-A difference was −6.25 percentage points (nominal 95 % confidence interval [−31.61, +19.57]). This interval is conditional on the observed rankings.
after: Table S4.  BrEaST performance at matched review counts

The original protocol specified the equal-review supplementary comparison closest to 20 % of BrEaST, giving 50/252 reviews per method. The additional 33- and 35-review rows are post hoc descriptive readouts at the already reported transferred-cutoff review volumes. They use the same original scores and risk-descending ranking, with lexicographic case-identifier tie-breaking. Low quality is reference Dice <0.70; each detection denominator is 16 and each review denominator is 252.

At K=50, among the 16 low-quality cases, both methods flagged 12, only A flagged 2, only B flagged 1, and neither flagged 1. The paired B-minus-A difference was −6.25 percentage points (nominal 95 % confidence interval [−31.61, +19.57]). This interval is conditional on the observed rankings.

At both K=33 and K=35, the low-quality paired counts are: both scores detect 10, A only 0, B only 3, and neither 3. Increasing the common budget from 35 to 50 adds four low-quality detections for A and none for B. These readouts describe the observed curves; no additional interval, hypothesis test or resampling analysis was performed. Machine-readable counts, denominators and paired outcomes are supplied in Breast Ultrasound Quality Control Matched Review Counts.csv.

before: The confidence threshold selected 20.45 % of internal patients and 13.89 % externally. Relative detection counts changed between transferred cutoffs and equal review at the 20 % target; a complete eight-budget analysis showed no uniformly better score. This manuscript uses this distinction to explain how an operating rule changes the interpretation of score comparisons. Three bootstrap routes and descriptive diagnostic-stratum accounting characterize its sampling and case-mix context without changing the prespecified H1–H3 analyses.
after: The confidence threshold selected 20.45 % of internal patients and 13.89 % externally. At matched counts of either 33 or 35 external reviews per score, confidence detected 10/16 low-quality masks and prompt disagreement detected 13/16; at 50 reviews, the counts were 14/16 and 13/16. The observed ordering therefore also changed with budget under the same equal-review ranking rule. This manuscript evaluates cutoff transfer alongside that ranking behavior, building on prior scoring and fixed-budget work. Three bootstrap routes and descriptive diagnostic-stratum accounting characterize sampling and case-mix context without changing the prespecified H1–H3 analyses.
